topics.name: Acids and bases: properties and indicators
pH: how strong are acids and bases
Salts: baking soda, washing soda, bleaching powder, plaster of Paris

questions.title: Turn the litmus back
questions.text: An aqueous solution turns red litmus blue. Excess addition of which of the following solutions would reverse the change?
steps: ① Red litmus → blue ⟹ the solution is basic
② To reverse it, we need an acid
③ NaOH, baking soda, slaked lime: all basic ✗
④ Excess HCl neutralises the base, then turns it acidic
∴ Hydrochloric acid → (b)
questions.remember: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue. Excess acid first neutralises a base, then makes the solution acidic.
questions.trap: Picking baking soda: it is a base (NaHCO₃ solution is basic), so it can't reverse a base.
questions.tryit: Which gas is given off when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?

questions.title: What is baking powder?
questions.text: Baking powder is a mixture of:
steps: ① Baking soda = sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃
② Baking powder = baking soda + a mild, dry, edible acid
③ That acid is tartaric acid (a solid)
④ Wet or heated: NaHCO₃ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O + Na⁺ salt
⑤ CO₂ bubbles make the cake soft and spongy
∴ NaHCO₃ + tartaric acid → (c)
questions.ans: Option (c) Sodium hydrogen carbonate + Tartaric acid
questions.remember: Baking soda: NaHCO₃. Baking powder: NaHCO₃ + tartaric acid. On heating or wetting it releases CO₂, which makes cakes soft and spongy.
questions.trap: Picking acetic acid: it's a liquid (vinegar). Baking powder is a dry powder, so its acid is solid tartaric acid.
questions.tryit: Why does a cake made with only baking soda taste bitter?
questions.tryans: Sodium carbonate forms on heating, and it is bitter

questions.title: Which salt is matched correctly?
questions.text:
Study the following table and select the correct option:
Salt · Acid used · Base used · Nature of salt
(a) NaCl · HCl · NaOH · Basic
(b) Na₂CO₃ · H₂CO₃ · NaOH · Neutral
(c) Na₂SO₄ · H₂SO₄ · NaOH · Acidic
(d) CH₃COONa · CH₃COOH · NaOH · Basic
steps: ① Strong acid + strong base ⟹ neutral salt
② Weak acid + strong base ⟹ basic salt
③ (a) HCl + NaOH: strong + strong ⟹ neutral, not basic ✗
④ (b) H₂CO₃ is weak ⟹ basic, not neutral ✗
⑤ (c) H₂SO₄ + NaOH ⟹ neutral, not acidic ✗
⑥ (d) CH₃COOH is weak, NaOH strong ⟹ basic ✓
questions.remember: Strong acid + strong base → neutral salt (pH 7). Weak acid + strong base → basic salt (pH > 7). Strong acid + weak base → acidic salt (pH < 7).
questions.trap: Picking (a): common salt is NEUTRAL, because HCl and NaOH are both strong.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 2 · Section 2.4.1 Family of salts
questions.tryit: NH₄Cl is made from HCl and NH₄OH. Acidic, basic or neutral?

questions.title: Copper oxide in dilute HCl
questions.text: To a small amount of copper oxide in a beaker, when we add dilute hydrochloric acid slowly with stirring, the change in the colour of the solution is due to the formation of:
opts: Copper(II) oxide, which is black in colour.
Copper(I) chloride, which is blue in colour.
Copper(II) chloride, which is blue-green in colour.
Copper(I) oxide, which is black in colour.
steps: ① Copper oxide is a metal oxide ⟹ basic
② Metal oxide + acid → salt + water
③ CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O
④ CuCl₂ is copper(II) chloride: blue-green
∴ Blue-green CuCl₂ → (c)
questions.ans: Option (c) Copper(II) chloride, which is blue-green in colour
questions.remember: Metal oxides are basic: metal oxide + acid → salt + water. CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O (blue-green solution).
questions.trap: Picking (a): copper oxide is what we STARTED with. The colour change comes from the new product, CuCl₂.
questions.tryit: What type of reaction is CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O?
questions.tryans: Neutralisation (a basic oxide reacting with an acid)

questions.title: Case study: the pH scale
questions.text:
The pH plays an important role in our daily life. Strength of acids and bases depends on the number of H⁺ ions and OH⁻ ions produced by them. The pH scale helps in predicting the strength of acids and bases by measuring hydrogen ion concentration.
(a) What type of indicator is used to predict how strong an acid or base is?
(b) Three solutions A, B and C showed pH 3, 5 and 7. Which has the highest concentration of H⁺ ions?
(c) What are strong acids and weak acids?
steps: ① (a) Universal indicator: a mix of indicators
② It shows a different colour for each pH, 0 to 14
③ (b) Lower pH ⟹ more H⁺ ions
④ pH 3 < 5 < 7 ⟹ A has the most H⁺
⑤ (c) Strong acid: gives MORE H⁺ ions, e.g. HCl
⑥ Weak acid: gives FEWER H⁺ ions, e.g. CH₃COOH
∴ Universal indicator · A · more vs fewer H⁺
questions.ans: (a) Universal indicator · (b) A (pH 3) · (c) Strong acids give more H⁺ ions (HCl); weak acids give fewer (CH₃COOH)
questions.remember: Litmus only says acid or base; universal indicator shows HOW strong (pH 0–14). Lower pH = more H⁺. pH 7 = neutral.
questions.trap: (b): picking C because 7 is the biggest number. On the pH scale, the SMALLEST pH has the most H⁺.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 2 · Section 2.3 How strong are acid or base solutions?
questions.tryit: Fresh milk has pH 6. As it turns into curd, does its pH rise or fall?
questions.tryans: It falls (curd is more acidic, lactic acid forms)

questions.title: Plaster of Paris: name, equation, uses
questions.text:
(a) Give the chemical name and formula of Plaster of Paris.
(b) Write the chemical equation of its preparation.
(c) Give any two uses of it.
steps: ① (a) Calcium sulphate hemihydrate
② Formula: CaSO₄·½H₂O
③ (b) Heat gypsum at 373 K
④ CaSO₄·2H₂O → CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O
⑤ (c) Plaster for fractured bones
⑥ Toys, decorations, smooth surfaces
∴ Name, formula, equation, two uses
questions.ans: (a) Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O · (b) CaSO₄·2H₂O → CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O (373 K) · (c) Plaster for fractures; toys and decorations
questions.remember: Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O, heated at 373 K, gives Plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O. Mixed with water, it sets back into hard gypsum.
questions.trap: Writing CaSO₄·H₂O or forgetting the temperature. It's HALF a water molecule (two formula units share one), at 373 K.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 2 · Section 2.4.5 Plaster of Paris
questions.tryit: Why should Plaster of Paris be stored in a moisture-proof container?
questions.tryans: Moisture makes it set into hard gypsum

questions.title: Give reasons: diluting acid, dry HCl, blue crystals
questions.text:
Give reasons:
(i) For dilution of an acid, acid is added into water and not water into acid.
(ii) Dry HCl gas does not turn blue litmus red, whereas dilute hydrochloric acid does.
(iii) Blue colour of copper(II) sulphate crystals turns white on heating.
steps: ① (i) Mixing acid and water is highly exothermic
② Water into acid boils and splashes; glass may crack
③ (ii) Acids show acidity only as H⁺ ions in water
④ Dry HCl gives no H⁺; with water: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻
⑤ (iii) Blue crystals: CuSO₄·5H₂O
⑥ Heat removes water of crystallisation ⟹ white CuSO₄
∴ Heat · H⁺ needs water · water lost
questions.ans: (i) Highly exothermic: water into acid boils and splashes · (ii) Dry HCl gives no H⁺ ions; H⁺ forms only in water · (iii) Heating removes water of crystallisation
questions.remember: Acid into water, slowly, with stirring. Acids show acidic behaviour only in water (H⁺ / H₃O⁺). CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue; anhydrous CuSO₄ is white.
questions.trap: (ii): writing 'dry HCl is weak'. HCl is a strong acid; dry, it simply has no H⁺ ions until water is present.
questions.tryit: Add a few drops of water to the white powder. What happens?
questions.tryans: It turns blue again (water of crystallisation returns)
